source_notes.observation: Terminology context only; the conditional guidance and synthetic examples are local editorial synthesis.

source_notes.location: Abstract; evaluation conditions and model selection
source_notes.observation: Terminology context only; the conditional guidance and synthetic examples are local editorial synthesis.

entries.meaning: Excluded from a named fitting, development or selection stage; not automatically excluded from all prior exposure.
entries.guidance: Specify held out from what and whether evaluation data influenced tuning or model selection.
entries.avoid: Calling a test set untouched after using it to select checkpoints.
conditions: The exclusion stage and partition are specified.
exceptions: A validation partition can be held out from gradient fitting while still used for selection; say so rather than banning the term.
evidence_required: Partition and stage-specific access protocol.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: validation data selects a checkpoint but is not used for gradient fitting.
examples: The validation split is held out from fitting and used for checkpoint selection.

counter_examples.text: The validation split is untouched by model development.
counter_examples.why: Checkpoint selection is part of model development.

source_notes.location: Data leakage and preprocessing guidance, retrieved search content; not a pinned software dependency
source_notes.observation: Terminology context only; the conditional guidance and synthetic examples are local editorial synthesis.

entries.meaning: Information crosses a declared evaluation or prediction-time boundary and can bias the claimed assessment.
entries.guidance: Identify the actual access path, boundary and effect rather than diagnosing leakage from high scores alone.
entries.avoid: Claiming leakage-free evaluation solely because filenames or partition labels differ.
conditions: The information access is disallowed by the stated evaluation protocol.
exceptions: A declared transductive or test-time-adaptation protocol may permit target inputs; do not silently judge it under an incompatible inductive protocol.
evidence_required: Access history, preprocessing/selection protocol and permitted target information.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: preprocessing statistics are fitted using the test split in an inductive evaluation.
examples: Test data influences fitted preprocessing statistics, violating the declared evaluation boundary.

counter_examples.text: There is no leakage because test labels were not used.
counter_examples.why: Unlabeled test inputs can still cross a disallowed fitting boundary.

entries.meaning: A proportion under a defined success criterion, trial denominator and aggregation rule.
entries.guidance: Distinguish pooled-trial success from a mean of per-task rates, especially with unequal trial counts.
entries.avoid: Reporting a macro task average as a pooled trial proportion.
conditions: A success criterion, denominator and averaging rule are available.
exceptions: Success can be graded or multi-stage; use the actual metric definition rather than forcing a binary rate.
evidence_required: Success criterion, trial counts, task weights and uncertainty unit.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: task A has 8/10 successes; task B has 1/2; macro averaging is used.
examples: The mean of the two task success rates is 65%.

counter_examples.text: The pooled success rate is 65%.
counter_examples.why: The pooled rate is 9/12, or 75%, not the macro average.

entries.meaning: An example of behavior supplied for imitation, instruction or evaluation, with a declared unit and source.
entries.guidance: Say whether a demonstration is an episode, a segment, a prompt example or another defined unit.
entries.avoid: Equating demonstration count with independent training runs, time steps or robot executions.
conditions: The example source and counting unit are specified.
exceptions: Language-model in-context demonstrations need not be robot trajectories; retain the relevant domain meaning.
evidence_required: Demonstrator source, episode/segment definition and data budget.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: ten expert episodes each contain 100 recorded steps.
examples: The dataset contains ten expert demonstrations, each with 100 recorded steps.

counter_examples.text: The dataset contains 1,000 independent demonstrations.
counter_examples.why: Time steps do not become independent behavior examples.

entries.meaning: A defined sequence of states, observations or actions; it can be generated, planned, logged or physically executed.
entries.guidance: Name the trajectory type and distinguish sampled plans from real executed episodes.
entries.avoid: Treating several sampled candidate trajectories as several independent real-world trials.
conditions: The sequence contents, origin and execution status are specified.
exceptions: A trajectory may be a segment rather than a complete episode; preserve the paper's definition.
evidence_required: Sequence definition and whether it was generated, logged or executed.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: eight candidate plans are sampled and one is executed.
examples: We sample eight candidate trajectories and execute one selected plan.

counter_examples.text: We perform eight robot trials.
counter_examples.why: Sampled plans are not physical executions.

entries.meaning: A sequence under a specified initialization and termination or truncation protocol.
entries.guidance: Report task, horizon, reset conditions and relation to trials or demonstrations where relevant.
entries.avoid: Equating repeated episodes from one checkpoint with independently trained policies.
conditions: Start and termination or truncation rules are declared.
exceptions: Continuing tasks can use artificial evaluation windows; identify the window rather than implying natural task termination.
evidence_required: Reset policy, horizon and replication unit.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: one checkpoint is evaluated for 20 episodes.
examples: We evaluate the checkpoint for 20 episodes.

counter_examples.text: The result averages 20 independent training runs.
counter_examples.why: Evaluation episodes and training runs are different units.

entries.meaning: Elapsed time between declared start and completion events for a request, decision or measured component.
entries.guidance: Name hardware, precision, batch, warm-up, synchronization and the timing boundary; distinguish mean from tail latency.
entries.avoid: Calling decoder-only timing sensor-to-action delay or inferring latency from FLOPs.
conditions: Timing events and measurement protocol are available.
exceptions: A component latency can be useful if labeled as that component; not every claim requires an end-to-end measurement.
evidence_required: Start/end events, measurement setup and aggregation.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: only decoder execution is timed at 12 ms.
examples: Decoder latency is 12 ms under the stated measurement setup.

counter_examples.text: The robot's sensor-to-action latency is 12 ms.
counter_examples.why: Sensing, preprocessing and communication are not in the measured interval.

entries.meaning: Completed declared work units per elapsed interval under a stated workload and concurrency regime.
entries.guidance: State tokens, requests, actions or another unit, including batch/concurrency and quality or latency constraints.
entries.avoid: Treating higher batch throughput as lower individual-request latency.
conditions: The counted work and elapsed interval are defined.
exceptions: Prefill, decoding and complete-request throughput measure different work; define the selected metric.
evidence_required: Work unit, concurrency, hardware, interval and any service constraints.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: batching raises requests per second, but per-request latency is not reported.
examples: Batching raises request throughput in the tested workload.

counter_examples.text: Batching makes every request faster.
counter_examples.why: Aggregate completion rate does not establish per-request latency.

entries.meaning: An explicit full boundary for a pipeline or optimization objective; end-to-end learning and end-to-end timing are different senses.
entries.guidance: Name the input/output or timing boundary and state excluded stages. Do not transfer the training sense into a runtime claim.
entries.avoid: Calling model-only execution an end-to-end deployment measurement.
conditions: The intended sense and endpoints are specified.
exceptions: A model can be trained end-to-end while deployed with unmeasured preprocessing; keep the two claims separate.
evidence_required: Optimization or measurement boundary, including excluded stages.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: the network is jointly trained, but timing covers its forward pass only.
examples: The network is trained end-to-end; the reported latency covers its forward pass only.

counter_examples.text: End-to-end training establishes the reported end-to-end system latency.
counter_examples.why: An optimization boundary is not a timing boundary.

source_notes.location: Abstract; aggregate scores, finite runs and uncertainty
source_notes.observation: Terminology context only; the conditional guidance and synthetic examples are local editorial synthesis.

entries.meaning: A defined uncertainty quantity, such as statistical estimation uncertainty, variability or predictive uncertainty; these senses differ.
entries.guidance: Identify the quantity, source and estimator; do not interchange across-run dispersion and calibrated predictive uncertainty.
entries.avoid: Calling a confidence interval an SD or an ensemble's spread a validated calibration guarantee.
conditions: The uncertainty source and summary are defined.
exceptions: A paper may discuss uncertainty qualitatively when no estimate exists, but must not fabricate an interval.
evidence_required: Uncertainty definition, estimator, replication unit and calibration evidence if claimed.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: intervals quantify uncertainty in an aggregate score estimated from finite runs.
examples: The interval summarizes estimation uncertainty in the aggregate score.

counter_examples.text: The interval proves that individual predictions are calibrated.
counter_examples.why: Aggregate estimation uncertainty does not establish predictive calibration.

entries.expression: Organize a paragraph around a reader question
entries.meaning: Paragraph organization follows the local explanatory task rather than an arbitrary sentence quota.
entries.guidance: Identify the question this paragraph answers and connect its supported statements to that answer.
entries.avoid: Listing unrelated dataset, architecture and runtime details in their discovery order.
conditions: The paragraph contains several facts whose relationship is unclear.
exceptions: A compact overview or enumerated contribution paragraph may intentionally answer several linked questions; do not force one rigid pattern.
evidence_required: A stated reader question and the author-supported relationships among the selected facts.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A paragraph explains how new documents enter a system; its weights remain fixed and its index is replaced.
examples: To incorporate new documents without updating model weights, we replace the retrieval index and generate answers conditioned on the retrieved passages.

counter_examples.text: We use an index. The model has many layers. We also tested several tasks.
counter_examples.why: Independent facts never answer how new documents enter the system.

source_notes.observation: Operation and result subsections are organized around distinct questions. This paragraph advice is an editorial inference, not a universal paper rule.

entries.expression: Connect an experimental result to the question it answers
entries.meaning: A result paragraph explains the supported implication of a comparison, not merely a sequence of scores.
entries.guidance: State the experimental question, retain the informative comparison and explain only the implication the design supports.
entries.avoid: Replacing a table with prose that repeats every number, or inventing a causal story to make the paragraph sound explanatory.
conditions: Reporting an experiment intended to distinguish a contribution, behavior or limitation.
exceptions: A descriptive dataset report may have no controlled hypothesis; describe the observed distribution without inventing one.
evidence_required: Question, comparison role, protocol and a bounded interpretation of the actual observation.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: An index is changed while weights and queries stay fixed; returned document identifiers are logged. No answer-correctness test is available.
examples: With model weights and queries fixed, replacing the index changes which documents are retrieved; this experiment tests retrieval responsiveness, not answer correctness.

counter_examples.text: The new index improves reasoning and guarantees accurate answers.
counter_examples.why: Document selection does not establish reasoning quality or answer correctness.

source_notes.observation: Named result subsections motivate bounded experimental questions. The synthetic test and its limitations are original, not results copied from RAG.

entries.expression: Match citation support to the particular attached claim
entries.meaning: A relevant paper title is not sufficient support for every clause in the sentence carrying its citation.
entries.guidance: Check the located source passage against each substantive clause; split differently supported assertions when needed.
entries.avoid: Using a method citation to support an unreported deployment or safety guarantee.
conditions: Adding or preserving a citation for a factual claim.
exceptions: A survey may support a broad synthesis when its reviewed scope actually covers it; no one-citation-per-clause quota is imposed.
evidence_required: Verified source identity, specific passage and a support relation for the attached claim.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A source describes retrieval-conditioned generation; it does not establish safety for medical deployment.
examples: The cited work describes retrieval-conditioned generation. Clinical deployment safety is not established by that method description.

counter_examples.text: Retrieval-conditioned generation is safe for clinical deployment, as established by the cited method paper.
counter_examples.why: The deployment claim exceeds the checked source passage.

source_notes.observation: This passage provides a method description, not a deployment-safety claim. The citation-support invariant is our editorial guard.

entries.meaning: Offer a supported but not decisive interpretation; the hedge does not create missing evidence.
entries.guidance: Name the observation and plausible interpretation while retaining alternative explanations.
entries.avoid: Hedging an unsupported causal assertion and treating it as supported.
conditions: Evidence licenses a tentative inference rather than a demonstrated conclusion.
exceptions: Use a direct observation verb for an established measurement, or prove for a valid theorem; do not hedge every statement.
evidence_required: Relevant observation and the limitations of its inference.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A single pilot run has fewer failures after a cache change, but other settings also differ.
examples: The pilot suggests a possible reduction in failures, although the changed settings prevent attribution to caching alone.

counter_examples.text: The pilot suggests that caching eliminates control failures.
counter_examples.why: A hedge does not license elimination or isolate caching.

source_notes.observation: The checklist asks authors to align claims and scope with results. It does not prescribe this verb; our wording advice is conditional.

entries.meaning: Make a specified operation available under stated conditions; not a synonym for measured improvement.
entries.guidance: Identify the enabled operation and the actual prerequisite it supplies.
entries.avoid: Converting interface availability into reliable performance or superior quality.
conditions: The design or implementation actually provides the named operation.
exceptions: Enable may legitimately describe a supported capability even without a superiority comparison; qualify design intent if not implemented.
evidence_required: Implemented operation and prerequisites; separate measurements for performance claims.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: An interface accepts a replacement document index without requiring weight changes.
examples: The interface enables index replacement without updating model weights.

counter_examples.text: The interface enables universally accurate generation.
counter_examples.why: An available update operation does not establish answer quality.

source_notes.observation: External-memory replacement is a useful capability distinction; the interface example and word-choice guidance are original.

entries.meaning: A time- and protocol-bounded comparison claim, not an intrinsic property of a method.
entries.guidance: State the benchmark, comparison set, metric and relevant budget; verify the comparison cutoff.
entries.avoid: Promoting the best score among two selected baselines into an unrestricted field-wide claim.
conditions: The covered comparison set and evaluated protocol warrant the stated ranking.
exceptions: A cited historical claim may be reported as such with its original scope and date; strongest observed baseline is preferable when coverage is incomplete.
evidence_required: Dated comparison coverage, matched protocol, metric direction, budgets and uncertainty where consequential.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A test compares A with B and C; no coverage of other published methods has been checked.
examples: A has the highest observed score among B and C under the tested protocol.

counter_examples.text: A is the state of the art in robot learning.
counter_examples.why: The field-wide comparison and other protocols were not checked.

source_notes.observation: Scope and experimental detail motivate this local comparison guard; the checklist does not certify a ranking.

entries.meaning: A claim about behavior as a specified workload or resource axis changes.
entries.guidance: Name the scaling axis, observed or derived relationship and tested range.
entries.avoid: Inferring scalability from one fast run or confusing parameter count with measured workload scaling.
conditions: There is evidence across the named axis or an explicitly conditional analytical bound.
exceptions: A theoretical complexity result may support an asymptotic claim without a large deployment; distinguish it from measured scaling.
evidence_required: Scaling axis, resource limits, range and measurement procedure or derivation assumptions.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Runtime is measured at several batch sizes on one device; multiple-device scaling was not tested.
examples: We measure runtime across the tested batch sizes on one device; this does not assess multi-device scaling.

counter_examples.text: The system scales to arbitrarily many devices.
counter_examples.why: The evaluation varies batch size, not device count or communication cost.

source_notes.observation: Resource reporting motivates a local scaling-scope guard; no universal threshold is inferred.

entries.meaning: A scoped originality claim relative to relevant prior work, not a decorative substitute for explaining the contribution.
entries.guidance: Describe the specific new distinction and check the relevant prior-art boundary.
entries.avoid: Calling a familiar module novel because this project uses it for the first time.
conditions: The identified distinction is supported by the authors' comparison with relevant work.
exceptions: A new combination or application may be a valid contribution without every component being new; describe its actual novelty.
evidence_required: Contribution identity and relevant prior-art review with an explicit search boundary.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: The project reuses a published retriever but introduces a separately supported index-update procedure.
examples: We reuse the published retriever and introduce the specified index-update procedure.

counter_examples.text: We introduce a novel retriever.
counter_examples.why: The novelty has been assigned to the reused component.

source_notes.observation: Accurate contribution scope motivates the guard. The checklist is not a prior-art search or proof of novelty.

entries.meaning: An attribution or causal-estimand claim whose identification depends on the design and assumptions.
entries.guidance: Specify the claimed causal relation, intervention or identification argument and remaining assumptions.
entries.avoid: Calling a correlation causal, or treating any component ablation as proof of the full proposed mechanism.
conditions: The evidence and identification assumptions support the named causal claim.
exceptions: Causal may name a model class or hypothesis without asserting an identified effect; distinguish those senses explicitly.
evidence_required: Estimand or mechanistic claim, design, confound control and identification assumptions.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Two changes are made together and success rises in the observed runs.
examples: Success rises after both changes; this comparison does not isolate either change's causal effect.

counter_examples.text: The routing change causally improves success.
counter_examples.why: The named change is not isolated and no identification argument is supplied.

entries.meaning: Task conditioning through the supplied context; distinguish prompt examples from gradient-based parameter updates.
entries.guidance: Name the context information and report any parameter updates separately.
entries.avoid: Calling prompt demonstrations fine-tuning or claiming that fixed weights imply absence of target information.
conditions: Describing a prompt-conditioned task procedure.
exceptions: A pipeline can combine in-context demonstrations with adapter training; state both rather than forcing one exclusive label.
evidence_required: Prompt contents and the actual update procedure.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Two labeled examples are placed in the prompt; no parameters are updated.
examples: We provide two labeled in-context examples without updating model parameters.

counter_examples.text: We fine-tune the model on two examples.
counter_examples.why: The examples condition the prompt rather than an optimization step.

source_notes.observation: The abstract distinguishes text demonstrations from gradient updates; no training-corpus exclusion is inferred.

entries.meaning: Generation conditioned on retrieved material; retrieval presence alone does not establish faithful support or factual correctness.
entries.guidance: Specify what is retrieved, how it conditions generation and what grounding or correctness tests are actually performed.
entries.avoid: Treating a returned passage or citation as proof that every generated statement is supported.
conditions: An actual retrieval step supplies information to generation.
exceptions: Retrievers or generators may also be trained or fine-tuned; retrieval and weight updates are separate axes.
evidence_required: Retrieval/generation data flow and separate support or correctness evaluation if claimed.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A generator receives retrieved passages, but statement-level support has not been evaluated.
examples: The generator conditions on retrieved passages; statement-level support remains unevaluated.

counter_examples.text: All generated statements are grounded because the system uses RAG.
counter_examples.why: Conditioning on material does not establish that the output is supported by it.

source_notes.observation: Retrieval and generation are connected operations. The fidelity warning is local editorial synthesis, not a reported RAG failure rate.

entries.meaning: Reward-directed policy learning from previously collected data without additional environment collection during the declared offline phase.
entries.guidance: State the dataset, learning objective and which phase excludes new interactions.
entries.avoid: Using offline to mean merely no internet access, or labeling every demonstration regression objective offline RL.
conditions: The described learning phase optimizes the stated reward-directed objective from fixed collected data.
exceptions: Offline pretraining followed by online fine-tuning is a hybrid pipeline; report each phase separately.
evidence_required: Dataset origin, objective, environment-collection schedule and phase boundary.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: An agent uses stored reward-labeled transitions, then collects new data in a later fine-tuning phase.
examples: We perform offline RL on the fixed transition dataset, followed by online fine-tuning.

counter_examples.text: The entire pipeline requires no new environment interactions.
counter_examples.why: The later online phase is silently removed.

source_notes.observation: The abstract identifies learning from previously collected data without additional online collection; detailed algorithm taxonomy was not reviewed.

entries.meaning: Learning behavior from demonstrations; an imitation objective is not automatically reward-based policy optimization.
entries.guidance: Identify the demonstrated behavior and actual loss; distinguish behavioral cloning from other imitation formulations.
entries.avoid: Calling action prediction RL solely because a learned policy is evaluated in an environment.
conditions: Training uses demonstration behavior to learn a policy or behavior model.
exceptions: Imitation can initialize an RL phase or use adversarial objectives; name the actual combination instead of equating all imitation with supervised regression.
evidence_required: Demonstration provenance, prediction targets, objective and later optimization phases.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A policy predicts demonstrated actions using only a supervised regression loss; no RL objective is optimized.
examples: We train an imitation policy by regressing demonstrated actions.

counter_examples.text: We train the policy with reinforcement learning.
counter_examples.why: Environment evaluation does not change the stated training objective.

source_notes.observation: Demonstrations supply action-prediction targets. The broader conditional terminology distinctions are local synthesis.

entries.meaning: Predicting or organizing multiple future actions as a chunk; prediction horizon and executed prefix are separate quantities.
entries.guidance: State chunk horizon, executed actions before replanning, observation cadence and controller level.
entries.avoid: Inferring a feedback-free controller from a multi-action prediction tensor.
conditions: The method predicts or executes a sequence of actions as a unit.
exceptions: A chunked policy can consume fresh observations every step, execute a prefix or combine overlapping predictions; the chunk size alone does not specify feedback cadence.
evidence_required: Prediction horizon, execution policy, observation schedule and low-level control loop.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A policy predicts six actions but consumes a fresh observation and recomputes its command at each step.
examples: The policy predicts six-action chunks and recomputes commands from fresh observations at every step.

counter_examples.text: The policy runs open-loop for six steps.
counter_examples.why: The feedback interval is one step, not the prediction horizon.

source_notes.observation: Chunk prediction and fresh observations need not share the same cadence; no source chunk size or success score is copied.

entries.meaning: At a specified controller level and interval, commands are not adjusted from feedback during that interval.
entries.guidance: Declare the control level, feedback signal and interval, rather than calling the entire robot open-loop.
entries.avoid: Ignoring low-level feedback when describing a high-level execution schedule.
conditions: Describing the absence of a particular feedback path during a bounded interval.
exceptions: A high-level action sequence may execute open-loop while a low-level servo tracks targets using feedback; both descriptions can be correct at their declared levels.
evidence_required: Command schedule, feedback paths and controller hierarchy.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: High-level targets are fixed for a chunk while the joint servo corrects tracking error.
examples: The high-level targets remain fixed during the chunk, while the joint servo uses tracking feedback.

counter_examples.text: The robot uses no feedback.
counter_examples.why: The statement erases the active low-level feedback loop.

source_notes.observation: Target prediction and low-level PID tracking are distinct; this operational definition is local guidance, not a universal control taxonomy.

entries.meaning: At the declared controller level, observed feedback affects subsequent commands; the feedback type and cadence matter.
entries.guidance: Specify the sensed quantity, update cadence and how observations change commands.
entries.avoid: Calling recorded video a visual feedback loop when it never affects commands.
conditions: A stated feedback path actually changes the control computation.
exceptions: Low-level proprioceptive feedback does not imply high-level visual replanning; identify the loop being described.
evidence_required: Feedback signal, causal data flow into command computation and timing.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Cameras log evaluation videos but only joint error affects servo commands.
examples: The joint servo uses closed-loop tracking; the logged camera images do not drive visual replanning.

counter_examples.text: The system performs closed-loop visual control.
counter_examples.why: The camera data is logged, not fed into the control computation.

source_notes.observation: Separate observation-conditioned policy commands from low-level tracking. The logging counter-example is original.

entries.meaning: Optimization using preference information; the objective, label source and use of explicit reward models must be specified.
entries.guidance: Distinguish direct preference objectives from reward-model fitting followed by RL; report human, synthetic or mixed label provenance.
entries.avoid: Equating every preference dataset with human feedback or every preference objective with an explicit reward-model pipeline.
conditions: Preferences influence the learning objective.
exceptions: A direct objective may imply a reward representation without fitting a separate reward network; different methods still require their own assumptions.
evidence_required: Objective, reference model, label provenance and actual optimization stages.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A direct pairwise objective trains on machine-labeled preference pairs without fitting a separate reward network.
examples: We optimize a direct preference objective on machine-labeled pairs, without fitting a separate reward network.

counter_examples.text: We train a human reward model and optimize it with RL.
counter_examples.why: Both the label provenance and the optimization stages have changed.

source_notes.observation: Direct policy optimization is distinguished from an explicit reward-model/RL pipeline; no universal equivalence beyond the stated assumptions is inferred.

entries.expression: Name the evaluated construct before interpreting its score
entries.meaning: A measurement of support, correctness, plausibility or mechanism faithfulness does not automatically measure the others.
entries.guidance: State the question, evaluation reference and unit; connect the score to that construct before drawing an implication.
entries.avoid: Using reader approval of an explanation as evidence that it captures the model's decision process.
conditions: Use when a metric label admits multiple interpretations or a conclusion crosses constructs.
exceptions: A named metric can be used after its construct and protocol have been defined nearby; a compact abstract need not repeat its full specification.
evidence_required: Operational construct, reference or oracle, units, and validation appropriate to the proposed interpretation.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Readers rate rationales as convincing; no model-process evaluation is conducted.
examples: Reader ratings measure rationale plausibility, not explanation faithfulness.

counter_examples.text: The convincing rationales faithfully explain the model's decisions.
counter_examples.why: No evidence about the prediction process was collected.

source_notes.observation: Distinguishes plausibility from reflecting prediction processes; the reader-question framing here is original editorial synthesis.
Correctness, fluency and citation quality are evaluated separately; shortcut outputs expose the risk of conflating these constructs.

entries.expression: Match the claim to the available evidence modality
entries.meaning: Input availability, visible evidence and annotation coverage constrain different claims; an unobserved property is not automatically absent.
entries.guidance: Identify the source view or reference used to verify the particular object, relation or statement; distinguish unsupported, contradicted and unassessed.
entries.avoid: Treating a missing caption mention or an occluded image region as proof that an object is absent.
conditions: Use for visual support checks and other incomplete references.
exceptions: A complete reference for the evaluated property can supply negative evidence; a partial view generally cannot.
evidence_required: Actual modality, reference coverage, visibility and the declared treatment of unknown cases.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A caption omits a mug; the reference captions are not an exhaustive object inventory.
examples: The caption does not mention a mug, but this does not establish absence from the image.

counter_examples.text: The image contains no mug because the reference caption does not mention one.
counter_examples.why: The caption inventory is incomplete; absence of a mention is not proof of object absence.

source_notes.observation: Object presence checks combine caption and segmentation evidence; the reference coverage limitation motivates this local writing distinction.

entries.expression: Separate failure stages before attributing a cause
entries.meaning: Plan validity, state-dependent skill feasibility and full execution are distinct stages; a gap between their rates is not a causal diagnosis.
entries.guidance: Explain which stage the evidence checks, then report what remains unresolved rather than assigning every downstream failure to one module.
entries.avoid: Inferring planner quality from execution alone or treating a stage-localized error as an isolated causal effect.
conditions: Use when evaluating staged language-to-action or planning-and-control systems.
exceptions: A controlled intervention or otherwise justified identification can support causal attribution; retain its actual scope.
evidence_required: Separate stage criteria and logs; comparable trial units; interventions if a cause is claimed.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Nine of ten plans are judged valid; six instructions finish physically; there is no controlled intervention.
examples: Planning validity and full execution are reported separately; their gap does not isolate the cause of execution failures.

counter_examples.text: The planner causes all four execution failures.
counter_examples.why: The cause is not isolated by a comparison of stage scores.

source_notes.location: Section 3 and Section 5 evaluation metric definitions
source_notes.observation: Skill relevance and affordance affect selection; plan validity and physical instruction completion are separate reported targets.

entries.meaning: A claim tied to a specified reference, modality or feasible action model; the intended sense and support relation must be recoverable.
entries.guidance: Name what is grounded in what, and whether the claim describes conditioning, alignment, verified support or estimated feasibility.
entries.avoid: Equating receipt of images or retrieved text with verification of every generated statement.
conditions: Use with a specified grounding sense and evidence appropriate to that sense.
exceptions: In grounded planning, a declared state-conditioned skill model may operationalize feasibility; this does not certify generated text or all real-world actions.
evidence_required: Grounding referent, operational procedure and any support or alignment evaluation actually performed.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: An answer model receives image inputs but output-to-region alignment is not evaluated.
examples: The answers are image-conditioned; visual grounding of individual statements is not tested.

counter_examples.text: Every answer is visually grounded because the model receives images.
counter_examples.why: Image input does not establish output alignment or statement support.

source_notes.observation: Text-conditioned detection and downstream grounding tasks have explicit visual targets; input conditioning alone is a different claim.
Grounding in state-conditioned robotic affordances uses a different referent from image-region or citation support.

entries.meaning: Either consistency with a specified source or fidelity of an explanation to a model process; these senses require different checks.
entries.guidance: Disambiguate the referent; distinguish unsupported-by-source from false-in-the-world, and convincing rationale from process fidelity.
entries.avoid: Using factually correct prose, source consistency or reader preference as a substitute for mechanism evidence.
conditions: Use only with a named target and an evaluation that tests the intended relation.
exceptions: Measured source consistency supports a bounded source-faithfulness claim, not necessarily world truth; a validated mechanism check can support its own process-faithfulness claim.
evidence_required: Located source support or a declared model-process test; evaluation scope and unresolved cases.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A date is independently verified outside the provided passage but absent from it; readers also approve the generated rationale; no process check is run.
examples: The date is externally verified but unsupported by the provided passage; the rationale is reader-approved, while explanation faithfulness is not evaluated.

counter_examples.text: The approved rationale is faithful to the model, and the unsupported date is false.
counter_examples.why: Reader approval tests plausibility, not process fidelity; unsupported-by-source is not equivalent to false.

source_notes.observation: Explanation faithfulness concerns prediction processes rather than human plausibility.
Support is operationalized relative to a declared reference knowledge source. The external-date example is original.

entries.meaning: No errors of a declared hallucination type under a stated evaluation; it is not a universal guarantee across types, prompts and conditions.
entries.guidance: Prefer a bounded observed-error statement when only a finite sample and limited reference coverage are checked.
entries.avoid: Turning zero detected object errors into guaranteed correctness of all attributes, relations and future outputs.
conditions: Use with a declared error taxonomy, evaluation scope, reference coverage and detection procedure.
exceptions: A finite evaluation can justify no observed errors under that protocol; a formal universal claim requires its own assumptions and proof, not just zero detections.
evidence_required: Checked error types, sample unit/count, reference coverage and adjudication or detector limitations.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Fifty captions are checked for unsupported object mentions against the declared object inventory; no such errors are detected; attributes are not checked.
examples: No object hallucinations are observed in the 50 evaluated captions; attribute errors are not assessed.

counter_examples.text: The system is hallucination-free for every image and description.
counter_examples.why: The universal statement exceeds both the tested error types and the finite sample.

source_notes.observation: CHAIR checks object hallucination using limited object/reference definitions, not every possible visual error.

entries.meaning: The fraction of evaluated generated factual units supported by a specified reference, with units and aggregation declared; not answer completeness or universal truth.
entries.guidance: State atomic-unit extraction, support reference and averaging. If calling a result FActScore, match its specified aggregation and disclose response/abstention handling.
entries.avoid: Calling a short answer complete merely because the facts it states are supported.
conditions: Use when generated facts are decomposed and checked against a declared reference.
exceptions: Custom protocols can count abstentions differently if named and specified; FActScore conditions its prompt-level average on responses, so do not silently relabel a different aggregation.
evidence_required: Fact units, per-response support checks, averaging, response rate and independent coverage targets if completeness is claimed.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A response has ten extracted atomic facts, eight supported by the reference; required-topic coverage is not measured.
examples: The reference supports 8 of 10 extracted atomic facts; answer completeness is not evaluated.

counter_examples.text: The answer is 80% complete because its factual precision is 80%.
counter_examples.why: Support precision over generated facts does not measure completeness of the requested answer.

source_notes.observation: Defines reference-relative support over atomic facts and an average conditional on responding; assumes unambiguous support and a suitable reference.

entries.meaning: Under the ALCE protocol, the average statement-level indicator that nonempty cited passages jointly support the entire statement; not retrieval recall or answer completeness.
entries.guidance: Declare statement segmentation, support procedure and empty-citation handling; keep this measure separate from citation precision and content correctness.
entries.avoid: Counting only statements that already have citations, or confusing coverage of emitted statements with coverage of the question.
conditions: Use with a specified citation-support evaluation; name the protocol when using ALCE's definition.
exceptions: Multiple passages may jointly support a statement; other citation-recall definitions are legitimate if their unit and denominator are explicit.
evidence_required: All evaluated statements, citation assignments, combined support checks and aggregation.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Four statements are evaluated; three have cited passages supporting their full content and one is uncited.
examples: The cited passages support three of four evaluated statements; ALCE-style citation recall is 75% under this segmentation.

counter_examples.text: Citation recall is 100% because all three cited statements are supported.
counter_examples.why: The uncited statement has been removed from the denominator.

source_notes.observation: A statement receives credit only with nonempty citations and support for its entire content from the combined cited passages.

entries.meaning: Under ALCE, per-citation credit requires full statement support and a citation that is not irrelevant; relevance accounts for individual or necessary joint support.
entries.guidance: Report the protocol and per-citation unit. Do not require every cited passage to support every clause alone, or penalize individually sufficient citations solely for redundancy.
entries.avoid: Redefining precision as the smallest possible citation set or assuming it certifies answer completeness.
conditions: Use with a declared per-citation support/relevance check.
exceptions: ALCE is not a minimal-set criterion: individually supporting citations can both be credited; joint support and other explicit precision protocols remain possible.
evidence_required: Full statement support, per-citation individual support and effect of removing a citation from the set.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: One statement has two citations; each passage alone supports its full content.
examples: Under the ALCE criterion, both citations can be relevant even though either would suffice alone.

counter_examples.text: Only one citation is correct because the second is redundant.
counter_examples.why: Both are individually supporting; redundancy alone does not make a citation irrelevant under this criterion.

source_notes.observation: Credit depends on statement recall and non-irrelevance. Individually sufficient citations are allowed; Appendix E limitations were not reviewed.

entries.meaning: A generated object mention unsupported by the declared visual object reference; a narrow error type whose vocabulary and annotation coverage must be specified.
entries.guidance: Declare how object mentions/presence are matched and whether the rate counts object instances or sentences containing an error.
entries.avoid: Equating an object-only metric with the absence of wrong attributes, relations or spatial reasoning.
conditions: Use when checking generated object mentions against a visual reference with defined coverage.
exceptions: Limited reference coverage requires qualification or adjudication of unknowns; an exhaustive reference can support stronger absence judgments within its scope.
evidence_required: Object vocabulary/matching policy, presence reference, unknown handling and object- or sentence-level denominator.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: An evaluated caption mentions a bicycle absent from the checked object reference; only object mentions are scored.
examples: The bicycle mention is an object hallucination under the checked reference; attributes and relations are outside this score.

counter_examples.text: The object-only check proves that the caption has no visual errors.
counter_examples.why: Unscored attributes and relations may still be wrong; this metric covers a narrower construct.

source_notes.observation: Distinguishes object-instance and sentence-level rates and uses bounded object/reference matching. No taxonomy or implementation is imported.

entries.meaning: In a declared localization sense, linking language referents to visual regions or objects and evaluating that link; distinguish this from merely conditioning on an image.
entries.guidance: Name the referent, visual target and localization protocol. Keep phrase localization distinct from general answer support or action feasibility.
entries.avoid: Inferring successful localization from image input, plausible text or an unvalidated attention plot.
conditions: Use when a language-to-visual-target relation is defined and the intended sense is explicit.
exceptions: Targets can be boxes, segmentation masks or other declared spatial representations; not every use of grounded in robotics refers to visual localization.
evidence_required: Query/target units, reference regions, matching thresholds and the alignment checks actually performed.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Twenty phrase queries have box annotations; twelve predicted regions meet the declared overlap threshold.
examples: Twelve of twenty phrase queries meet the declared box-overlap criterion for visual grounding.

counter_examples.text: All answers are visually grounded because images enter the model.
counter_examples.why: Image input alone does not verify localization or answer support.

source_notes.location: v2 abstract; author project pretraining/box-evaluation summary
source_notes.observation: Phrase/object alignment and downstream referring-expression tasks provide context for this bounded localization sense; the full PDF body was not reviewed.

entries.meaning: The state-, agent- and skill-dependent possibility of achieving an action outcome; an estimated skill value can operationalize it but is not an unconditional guarantee.
entries.guidance: Specify the skill, current state and meaning of the feasibility score; distinguish semantic usefulness from physical executability.
entries.avoid: Treating a language model's preference for a useful action as evidence that the robot can perform it now.
conditions: Use with a declared agent/skill/state relation or a specified affordance estimator.
exceptions: A task-specific feasibility definition or calibrated probability may be appropriate when validated; not every value function is a calibrated probability.
evidence_required: Agent and skill library, state information, score meaning, training/evaluation scope and calibration if probabilistic claims are made.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: A language score ranks fetch-cup highly, but the state-conditioned skill-value estimate is low.
examples: The instruction favors fetch-cup semantically, while its estimated robotic affordance is low in the current state.

counter_examples.text: The robot is guaranteed to fetch the cup because the action is linguistically appropriate.
counter_examples.why: Semantic relevance is not a physical guarantee, and an estimated skill score has its own uncertainty.

source_notes.observation: Combines language usefulness with state-conditioned skill value/affordance; estimated feasibility and semantic relevance are different roles.

entries.meaning: Completion of every ordered subgoal under a stated chain protocol; full-chain success, successful-prefix length and conditional stage success are different summaries.
entries.guidance: Specify chain length/order, progression/termination criteria, resets and denominator; never substitute marginal single-task rates for chain success.
entries.avoid: Averaging isolated task scores or dividing last-stage completions by survivors while calling it full-chain success.
conditions: Use when subgoals are evaluated as an ordered sequence with declared progression and state carryover.
exceptions: Mean successful prefix length and conditional stage rates are valid complementary measures when labeled; interrupted or reset protocols need their own definitions.
evidence_required: Number of initial chains, stage success criteria, survivor counts, reset/termination rules and aggregation.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: Twelve four-task chains stop at first failure without intermediate resets; successful prefix counts are 12, 9, 6, 3.
examples: Full-chain success is 3 of 12 initial chains (25%); last-stage success conditional on reaching it is 3 of 6 (50%).

counter_examples.text: Full-chain success is 50% because three of the six chains reaching the last task complete it.
counter_examples.why: The denominator is conditional survivors, not all initial chains.

source_notes.observation: Sequential progression depends on subgoal completion; single-goal and chain rollouts are separate protocols. The four-task arithmetic is original, not CALVIN results.

entries.meaning: A domain-relative description of extended temporal dependency or sequential decision depth; prediction length, execution duration and task-chain depth are different axes.
entries.guidance: State the evaluated horizon axis and task dependence; explain what makes it long in this setting rather than using a universal step threshold.
entries.avoid: Claiming demonstrated long-horizon task completion from a long predicted action chunk or many unrelated short trials.
conditions: Use with a defined temporal or sequential axis and an appropriate evaluation for the claimed capability.
exceptions: A domain-specific time/decision scale may justify the label without task chains; no fixed chain length or number of seconds applies to all domains.
evidence_required: Duration/decisions/subgoals, dependencies, feedback and resets, and actual task-completion evidence.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: An evaluation uses four dependent subgoals without intermediate resets; the policy predicts 32-action chunks, but that prediction length is not the task definition.
examples: We evaluate four-subgoal task chains with state carried between subgoals; the 32-action prediction horizon is reported separately.

counter_examples.text: A 32-action output proves successful long-horizon task execution.
counter_examples.why: The prediction horizon does not establish the duration, dependency depth or success of physical task execution.

source_notes.observation: Language-conditioned sequential tasks provide an operational long-horizon setting, not a universal numerical threshold.
Prediction chunks and observation-conditioned execution are distinct. This source was read in the earlier curation round.

entries.expression: Preserve preconditions, action order and required steps in reproducibility instructions
entries.meaning: In instructions intended for execution, preconditions and required sequence are part of the technical meaning, not optional stylistic framing.
entries.guidance: Make the action target and its precondition recoverable before the reader acts; keep required steps in the procedure rather than an optional note. Preserve supplied warnings and literal commands without executing them.
entries.avoid: Moving a validation step after an irreversible action, broadening a deletion target or burying a required safeguard in a note.
conditions: Apply to requested reproducibility steps or operation instructions associated with a research artifact, not to every descriptive method sentence.
exceptions: Declared simultaneous or independent actions need not be serialized; a prior unambiguous precondition can apply to a whole block. A scientific description need not become imperative instructions.
evidence_required: Author-supplied preconditions, required actions, actual dependencies, targets and any existing warnings; do not invent safety guarantees.
entries.example_context: Synthetic: The checkpoint checksum must be verified before intermediate shards are removed; the final archive must be retained.
examples: After verifying the checkpoint checksum, remove only the intermediate shards; retain the final archive.

counter_examples.text: Remove all shards and then verify the checkpoint checksum.
counter_examples.why: The order and target change: verification occurs too late and the final archive is no longer protected.

source_notes.location: SKILL.md operating rules 1, 6-7; references/essential-rules.md passage priorities and preservation; references/source-boundary.md verification boundary
source_notes.observation: Text function, preconditions and required actions are relevant design ideas. The research-specific checksum example is original; numeric STE limits, warning labels and rule-ID authority are not imported.
